name: Giardia duodenalis

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Cyst: about 8–19 µm long, oval, with two nuclei when immature and four when mature; axonemes and median bodies may be visible.
Trophozoite: 10–20 µm, pear-shaped, with two nuclei, a ventral attachment disk and eight flagella.

transmission.detail: Ingested cysts excyst in the small intestine; trophozoites multiply and attach to mucosa, then encyst before fecal passage.

life_cycle.detail: A host ingests cysts through fecal–oral exposure.
Cysts release trophozoites in the small intestine.
Cysts form during intestinal transit and pass in stool, enabling transmission.

hosts: Humans and other mammals; assemblages differ in host association. No intermediate host.
distribution: Worldwide, including Thailand; water, food and close-contact transmission are relevant.
clinical_significance: Diarrhea, bloating, steatorrhea and malabsorption; asymptomatic carriage occurs.
specimen: Cysts and trophozoites in stool; trophozoites are more often found in loose specimens.
diagnostics: Fresh saline mounts demonstrate motility; iodine highlights cyst structures.
Permanent trichrome or iron-hematoxylin smears near 1000× reveal nuclei; antigen or molecular assays can supplement microscopy.
differential_diagnosis: Assemblages cannot be inferred from morphology.
Preserve cyst/trophozoite and stain labels; yeast lacks the characteristic paired nuclei and internal fibrils.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated
description: Giardia duodenalis — Giardia intestinal flagellate. Diarrhea, bloating, steatorrhea and malabsorption; asymptomatic carriage occurs.

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
